turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1
    time, Heat treatment step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2
    temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling
    rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time,
    Heat treatment step 3 cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 3 time, Secondary treatment step 4
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield
    strength at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would prioritize candidates with **low-temperature second-stage tempering and no subsequent thermal exposure**.

The strongest relevant patterns in the training data are:

- For a 13% Cr steel containing 0.12% C and 0.2% Ti, tempering at **250°C gave 930 MPa**, compared with **780 MPa at 540°C**.
- A related 13% Cr, 0.4% C steel achieved **1,390 MPa at 500°C**, while related samples tempered at 550–600°C were substantially weaker. Carbon content matters, so that absolute strength should not be transferred directly to these 0.2% C candidates.
- Across several other composition-matched series, lower tempering temperatures generally preserve higher strength. Most pool candidates tempered at 715–740°C are therefore less promising.

Using those composition-and-treatment comparisons, my ranking is:

| Rank | Candidate | Main reason |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | **c021** | 200°C temper; Ni/Mn/Si-bearing composition; no later exposure |
| 2 | **c015** | 200°C temper and 0.205% C; no later exposure |
| 3 | **c017** | Same composition as c021, tempered at 300°C |
| 4 | **c018** | Same composition as c015, tempered at 300°C |
| 5 | **c006** | 450°C temper; preferred over the higher-temperature alternatives |

This is a **comparison-based prediction**, not a validated fitted-model result. The exact ordering of the two composition families—and the fifth-place choice versus c014—is less certain than the preference for this low-temperature group.

Final: c021, c015, c017, c018, c006
